public_rationale: The sentence is a broad characterisation, not a checkable fact. It says most AI tool sales are pitched on future potential to buyers who will never use them, and that Altman manipulates and frightens the powerful. No dataset measures the share of all AI sales pitched on future capability. 'Never really use them' is partly a prediction and depends on whether buyers means organisations or people. 'Manipulate, pester and terrify' describes motive. Usage figures such as ChatGPT's 400 million weekly users bear on one piece but cannot settle the 'for the most part' claim, so no fair support or contradiction test exists.
limitations: Parts of the claim, such as enterprise seat utilisation, could be studied in isolation, but that would not test what he actually said.

our_interpretation: The claim mixes three things. One is the content of sales pitches across all AI tools ('based on what they might do in the future'). Another is a forecast about buyers' future behaviour ('will never really use them'). The third is a description of Altman's motives and their effect on 'those in power' ('manipulate, pester and terrify').

No public dataset measures what share of all AI tool sales rest on future capability rather than current use. 'Those in power' and 'never really use them' also have no plain, measurable boundary. Whether buyers means purchasing organisations or the people inside them changes the answer.
Public usage data (for example, hundreds of millions of weekly ChatGPT users) speaks only to part of the claim and cannot settle the 'for the most part' sales characterisation.
criteria.support_condition: Not adjudicable. It would need representative data showing most AI tool sales are pitched mainly on future capabilities to buyers who do not use them.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Not adjudicable. It would need representative data showing most AI tool sales rest on current capabilities and that buyers actually use what they buy.
